segments.speakEn: Everything around you that can be measured or counted is a quantity. Quantities come in two kinds. Discrete quantities are separate, countable items with specific values.

segments.speakEn: A digital system is an electronic system that uses only two values: 0 and 1. These two values are called binary digits, or bits for short. 0 represents OFF, LOW, or FALSE.

segments.speakEn: 1 represents ON, HIGH, or TRUE. Why only two values? Because it is easy for an electronic circuit to tell "voltage present" from "no voltage".

actions.text: Worked example
Why is copying digital data "accurate"?
Step 1: A song is stored as bits, for example 10110010… Step 2: When you copy it to a USB, the computer copies each bit exactly: 1 stays 1, 0 stays 0.
Step 3: Even after 100 copies the bits are identical, so the song sounds the same.
An old cassette tape (analog) loses a little quality every time it is copied.

segments.speakEn: Here is a worked example. Pause the lecture and try it on paper before you continue. Why is digital more resistant to noise? Step 1: Suppose a wire carries 5 V for HIGH and 0 V for LOW.
segments.speakUr: اب ایک حل شدہ مثال۔ وقفہ کر کے کاغذ پر خود کوشش کریں۔

actions.text: Worked example
Why is digital more resistant to noise?
Step 1: Suppose a wire carries 5 V for HIGH and 0 V for LOW.
Step 2: Noise adds a small error, so 5 V arrives as 4.6 V and 0 V arrives as 0.3 V.
Step 3: The receiver only asks "Is it closer to HIGH or LOW?" 4.6 V is still read as 1 and 0.3 V is still read as 0.

segments.speakEn: Boolean algebra was developed by the English mathematician George Boole. It is a kind of algebra that deals with only two values: TRUE (1) and FALSE (0). It is the foundation of digital electronics and computer programming — every if condition in a program is a small piece of Boolean algebra.

actions.text: Worked example
Using a law: Simplify Y = A'B + AB.
Step 1: Both terms contain B, so take B out: Y = B(A' + A).
Step 2: A' + A = 1 (a variable OR its opposite is always 1).
Step 3: Y = B · 1 = B.

segments.speakEn: Logic gates are electronic circuits that perform Boolean operations. They take one or more input bits and produce one output bit. They are the building blocks of all digital systems — a processor contains billions of them.

segments.speakEn: The three basic gates match the three basic operations: the AND gate, the OR gate and the NOT gate (also called an inverter). A B Y A B Y A Y AND: Y = A · B OR: Y = A + B NOT: Y = A' Symbols of the basic gates. segments.speakEn: A Karnaugh map (K-map) is a graphical tool used to simplify Boolean expressions. It is a grid of cells — one cell for each row of the truth table. The cells are arranged so that neighbouring (adjacent) cells differ by only ONE bit.

segments.speakEn: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a system in which physical devices are connected to the Internet and can collect and share data to perform tasks automatically. The "things" are ordinary objects — watches, cameras, cars, fans, water pumps — that have been given sensors and an internet connection so they can "talk" to each other and to us. Source example: A smartwatch collects your heart-rate data and sends it to your mobile phone, where it is displayed.

segments.speakEn: Digital literacy is the ability to understand and use digital devices, the internet, and online tools in a safe, effective, and responsible manner. Look at the three key words: Safe – you protect yourself and others online (for example, you do not share passwords or private details). Effective – you get the job done well (for example, you find the right information quickly).

segments.speakEn: A simulation is a computer-based model of a real situation. Variables (the things that can change, like speed, temperature or number of people) can be changed to see what happens. Simulations are highly useful when real experiments are costly, risky or difficult to perform.

actions.text: Learn it
A simulation is a computer-based model of a real situation.
Variables (the things that can change, like speed, temperature or number of people) can be changed to see what happens.
Simulations are highly useful when real experiments are costly, risky or difficult to perform.

segments.speakEn: Examples: a flight simulator for training pilots (real crashes are dangerous) a traffic simulation to test what happens if a new signal is added (changing real roads is costly) a weather model to predict a cyclone (you cannot experiment with real weather).

In many cases, evaluating clarity is even more important than making the algorithm slightly faster.
A clear algorithm is easier to maintain, debug and extend over time.
